welcome9.q_kicker: The questions behind every rotation decision
welcome9.q_h: Start with the money and the bad year
welcome9.q_p: Each answer is worked out for your own field from decades of real weather, USDA prices and costs you can change, and crop-insurance records for your county (US).
welcome9.q1: How much could I earn, after costs?
welcome9.q1_p: Return per acre for each rotation, with seed, fertilizer, chemicals and other input costs shown line by line, on your acres. Put in your own yields, prices and costs any time.
welcome9.q1_ex: Iowa example: {{name}} makes about {{v}} an acre in a typical year, over operating costs.
welcome9.q2: What happens in a bad year?
welcome9.q2_p: The 1-in-10 bad year, dry years, low prices, the chance of losing money and the worst year on record, next to the typical year.
welcome9.q2_ex: Iowa example: in a bad year (1 in 10) {{name}} still makes about {{v}} an acre over operating costs.
welcome9.q2_ex_neg: Iowa example: in a bad year (1 in 10) {{name}} loses about {{v}} an acre over operating costs.
welcome9.q3_p: The comparison that answers both: every rotation your field, equipment and markets allow, side by side on earnings, bad-year risk, soil and water, ranked by what matters to you.
welcome9.q3_ex: Iowa example: {{n}} rotations tested; for this farmer's priorities the top one is {{name}}.
welcome9.q4: Will it cut pests and disease?
welcome9.q4_p: A benefit of rotating: each option is checked against rotation rules from extension research, such as crops that share pests back to back, the same plant family too often, and how often the rotation breaks a pest cycle.
welcome9.q4_ex: Iowa example: {{best}} breaks the pest cycle in {{b}} of crop changes, against {{a}} for the rotation grown today.
welcome9.q_ex_live: Live from FarmSmart's model for a real field in Story County, Iowa.
welcome9.farm_p: Add your fields one at a time, then see them side by side: what the whole farm could earn, its bad year, the crop mix each year, and a plan for each field that fits the rest.
welcome9.more_h: Soil, water and the decades ahead
welcome9.worries: Input costs and weather are farmers' top worries (Purdue/CME Ag Economy Barometer 2026; McKinsey Global Farmer Insights 2024).

u9money.head_sub_gm: What each option could earn on this field a year, after the costs of growing the crop. Land, machinery and your own labour are not taken off: turn on fixed costs under “Show cost details” to see net profit.
u9money.head_sub_net: What each option could earn on this field a year, after operating costs and fixed costs (land, machinery, labour and overhead).
u9money.evidence: Based on {{s}} real growing seasons ({{y0}}–{{y1}}) × {{p}} price years ({{p0}}–{{p1}}).
u9money.evidence_seq: Based on {{s}} real weather sequences starting {{y0}}–{{y1}} × {{p}} price years ({{p0}}–{{p1}}).
u9money.evidence_noprice: Based on {{s}} real weather sequences starting {{y0}}–{{y1}}, with one set of prices (no price history here).
u9money.counted_oh_off: Not counted now: fixed costs (land, machinery, labour, general overhead). Turn them on under “Show cost details”.
u9money.counted_cover: Cover crop seed and planting ({{v}} an acre each cover year)
u9money.counted_n: Fertilizer N saved after soybeans or a legume cover (taken off costs)
u9money.counted_pay: Conservation payment for cover crops ({{v}} an acre)
u9money.counted_loss: Losses from hail, flood, wind and other causes, from crop-insurance records
u9money.counted_src: Cost line names from USDA ERS Commodity Costs and Returns.
u9money.loss_h: How losses are counted (no double counting)
u9money.loss_p1: Drought, heat and frost during the season are already in the {{s}} simulated weather years: the crop model grows each crop through that weather, so a dry or hot year already shows as a lower yield.
u9money.loss_p2: Losses the weather model does not simulate (hail, flood, too much rain, wind, insects, disease and others) are taken from USDA crop-insurance records for {{county}}, one cause at a time: each cause hits a simulated year with the chance seen in the records, and costs the average loss per acre of the years it hit.
u9money.loss_p3: Insurance records of drought, heat and in-season frost are left out, so nothing is counted twice. Insurance only pays above the deductible, so real losses were somewhat larger than these records.
u9money.loss_off: Losses from insurance records are switched off now (see “Test bad years”).
u9money.loss_none: No crop-insurance loss records were found for this county, so only the weather in the simulated years is counted.
u9money.evidence_full: Based on {{s}} real weather sequences (starting {{y0}}–{{y1}}, weather from {{c0}}–{{c1}}) × {{p}} price years ({{p0}}–{{p1}}) = {{n}} combinations per option.
u9money.yh_aria: {{crop}}: published yields in {{where}}, {{y0}}–{{y1}}, with the trend line
u9money.yh_trend: Straight-line trend: {{v}} {{u}} in {{y}}, rising {{slope}} {{u}} a year.
u9money.yh_use_above: The yield in use here ({{v}} {{u}}) is {{pct}}% above that trend for {{y}}.
u9money.yh_use_below: The yield in use here ({{v}} {{u}}) is {{pct}}% below that trend for {{y}}.
u9money.yh_use_same: The yield in use here ({{v}} {{u}}) is close to that trend.
u9money.yh_cv: Once the trend is taken out, yields swing about {{pct}}% from year to year.
u9money.yh_scale: County average, not your field: shown for context, never used as your field's yield.
u9money.bm_how: “Use these numbers” fills this crop's cost lines with the budget's (lines the budget does not have are set to 0) and its fixed costs (land, machinery, labour). Your yield and price are not changed.
u9money.bm_done: In use: {{label}}, operating costs {{op}} an acre and fixed costs {{fixed}}.
u9money.bm_extra: These budget lines have no USDA line of their own, so they are in the operating total but not in a line: {{list}}. Changing any single line goes back to adding up the lines.
u9money.bm_yield: The budget assumes {{v}} {{u}}; your yield above is unchanged.
u9money.storm_damage: Reported crop damage {{v}} in total, over {{n}} years.
u9money.storm_note: Reported events; reporting varies by county and decade, and crop damage is often left at zero. These are not your field's losses: hail, wind and flood losses in the numbers come from crop-insurance records, and drought, heat and frost are already in the simulated weather years.
